hints: Think about what type of starting material $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{22}$ is and what type of products $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ are, then recall the industrial process that breaks long alkanes into shorter alkanes plus alkenes.
walkthrough:
Link the formulas to alkane and alkene**
$\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{22}$ fits $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$, so it is a long chain alkane. $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ fits $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}$ and decolourises bromine, so it is an alkene. You are going from a large saturated molecule to a smaller unsaturated one by splitting the chain.
Final answer: cracking

hints: Since all three decolourise bromine they must all contain $\text{C}=\text{C}$, so try moving the double bond position and branching the carbon skeleton while keeping $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$.
walkthrough:
Build the three different carbon skeletons for $\text{C}_4$ alkenes**
Keep four carbons and one $\text{C}=\text{C}$ in every drawing. First make a straight chain with the double bond at the end: $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Then keep the straight chain but move the double bond to the middle: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$. Then branch the chain to give three carbons in a row with a methyl branch on the double bond carbon: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (but-1-ene) and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$ (but-2-ene) and $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$ (methylpropene)

hints: Recall what must be the same and what must be different for any type of stereoisomerism, focusing on molecular formula versus arrangement in space.
Think about why rotation cannot happen around $\text{C}=\text{C}$ and how that locks substituents on each carbon into fixed positions.
walkthrough:
Separate what is identical from what is different**
Picture two molecules that have exactly the same atoms joined in exactly the same order. For geometrical isomers the connectivity is identical, so the molecular formula and structural formula match. What differs is how the groups sit in space around the double bond.

Explain why the positions are locked**
A $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond contains a pi bond that would break if you twisted one end relative to the other. Because rotation is restricted, the two groups on each $\text{C}$ of the double bond are frozen on one side or the other, giving cis and trans (or E/Z) arrangements.
Final answer: Molecules with the same molecular and structural formula but different arrangement in space due to restricted rotation about the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond.

hints: Identify A as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$ and recall that the pi electrons of $\text{C}=\text{C}$ act as the nucleophile that attacks the partially positive H of $\text{HBr}$.
Think about how $\text{HBr}$ is polarised as $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ and where the pair of electrons from the $\text{H}-\text{Br}$ bond must go when H adds to carbon.
Consider what type of intermediate is left on carbon after H has added, and what charge it carries.
Think about how the $\text{Br}^{-}$ ion with its lone pairs then behaves toward that positively charged carbon.
walkthrough:
Start with the correct alkene**
Only but-2-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$, can show geometrical isomerism because each $\text{C}$ of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ carries two different groups ($\text{CH}_3$ and H). Draw it displayed with all atoms and bonds shown.

Show electrophilic attack by HBr**
The $\text{C}=\text{C}$ is electron rich. Draw $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ with H pointing toward the double bond. Push a curly arrow from the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ pair to the $\text{H}^{\delta+}$. At the same time push a curly arrow from the $\text{H}-\text{Br}$ bond onto Br, giving $\text{Br}^{-}$ and a carbocation $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}^{+}\text{CH}_3$.

Form the carbocation clearly**
One carbon of the original double bond now bonds to H, the other becomes $\text{C}^{+}$ with only six electrons and a positive charge. For A both possible carbocations are identical secondary carbocations, so just draw one.

Capture the carbocation with bromide**
Draw $\text{Br}^{-}$ with full octet of lone pairs and a negative charge. Push a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{Br}^{-}$ to the $\text{C}^{+}$ to form the $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond, giving 2-bromobutane $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_3$.

Final answer: Displayed formula of A: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$.
Step 1: curly arrow from $\text{C}=\text{C}$ to $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$, with curly arrow from $\text{H}-\text{Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}$ to form $\text{Br}^{-}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}^{+}\text{CH}_3$ carbocation.
Step 2: lone pair on $\text{Br}^{-}$ attacks $\text{C}^{+}$, curly arrow from $\text{Br}^{-}$ to $\text{C}^{+}$ to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_3$.

hints: Picture a tetrahedral carbon in 3D and ask yourself how many different atoms or groups must be attached for the mirror image to be non-superimposable.
walkthrough:
Visualise the tetrahedral carbon**
Imagine a central carbon with four single bonds pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron. If all four attached groups are different, there is no plane of symmetry and the mirror image cannot be superimposed. That carbon is the chiral centre.
Final answer: An atom (carbon) with four different atoms or groups attached.

hints: B gives one chiral bromobutane (X) and one achiral bromobutane (Y) on addition of HBr, so test which $\text{C}_4$ alkene can add H and Br in two different ways to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_3$ versus $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from X and Y**
X has a chiral centre and is formed in higher yield, which fits 2-bromobutane $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHBrCH}_3$ where C2 carries H, Br, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Y with no chiral centre fits 1-bromobutane $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$. Only $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, but-1-ene, can give that pair by adding H to either end of the double bond.

hints: Focus on C2 of 2-bromobutane $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ as the chiral centre and recall how to show tetrahedral 3D shape with solid, wedged and dashed bonds.
Think about the relationship between the two optical isomers as mirror images, so consider swapping any two groups or drawing the mirror reflection.
walkthrough:
Draw one enantiomer in 3D**
Put C2 in the centre bonded to $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, Br and H. Show 3D shape correctly, for example two bonds as normal lines, one as a solid wedge coming out and one as a dashed wedge going back. Do not draw the two in-plane bonds opposite each other at 180 degrees.

Draw the non-superimposable mirror image**
Keep the same four groups on C2 but swap the positions of two groups, for example swap H and Br between wedge and dash, or draw the exact mirror reflection. The two structures must not be superimposable.

Final answer: Two 3D structures of $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ centred on C2 with four groups: $\text{H}$, $\text{Br}$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, drawn with wedge, dash and two solid bonds, one the mirror image of the other (or with two groups swapped).

hints: Compare the carbocation leading to X (secondary, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}^{+}\text{CH}_3$) with the carbocation leading to Y (primary, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^{+}$) and decide which positive carbon is better stabilised.
Recall how alkyl groups push electron density toward a neighbouring positive charge and what this electron donating effect is called.
walkthrough:
Identify the two competing intermediates**
Adding $\text{H}^{+}$ to C1 of but-1-ene gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}^{+}\text{CH}_3$, a secondary carbocation with two alkyl groups attached to $\text{C}^{+}$. Adding $\text{H}^{+}$ to C2 gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^{+}$, a primary carbocation with only one alkyl group. The secondary ion is more stable and forms faster.

Explain the stabilisation by alkyl groups**
Alkyl groups are electron releasing by the positive inductive effect. They push electron density toward the electron deficient $\text{C}^{+}$, spreading out and lowering the charge density. More alkyl groups means greater stabilisation, so the pathway via the secondary carbocation dominates and X is the major product.

Final answer: The intermediate carbocation leading to X is secondary and more stable than the primary carbocation leading to Y.
This is due to the electron releasing (positive) inductive effect of the alkyl groups which reduces the charge density on $\text{C}^{+}$.

hints: By elimination the remaining $\text{C}_4$ alkene is the branched one $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$, so apply IUPAC rules for the longest chain containing $\text{C}=\text{C}$.
walkthrough:
Name the leftover isomer**
A was but-2-ene and B was but-1-ene, so C must be the branched alkene $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$. The longest chain through the double bond has three carbons (propene) with a methyl substituent on C2, giving methylpropene.
Final answer: methylpropene or methylprop-1-ene or 2-methylpropene or 2-methylprop-1-ene

hints: Draw C as $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$ and add H to one carbon and Br to the other in the first way round, then reverse them for the second product.
Remember displayed means showing every atom and every bond, so check that neither product has a carbon with four identical sets of groups that would make it chiral, as stated.
walkthrough:
Add HBr across the double bond both ways**
For $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$, adding H to $\text{CH}_2$ and Br to the central C gives $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CBrCH}_3$. This is the Markovnikov major product via the tertiary carbocation. Adding H to the central C and Br to $\text{CH}_2$ gives $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Br}$.

Draw fully displayed**
Show every C, H and Br with all bonds: for the first isomer show the central carbon with two $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bonds to $\text{CH}_3$, one $\text{C}-\text{C}$ to $\text{CH}_3$ and one $\text{C}-\text{Br}$. For the second show $\text{CH}$ connected to two $\text{CH}_3$ groups and to $\text{CH}_2$ which connects to Br. Neither contains a carbon with four different groups, consistent with no chiral centre.

Final answer: Product 1: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CBrCH}_3$ displayed as central C bonded to Br and two $\text{CH}_3$ groups and to $\text{CH}_3$ (2-bromo-2-methylpropane).
Product 2: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Br}$ displayed as $\text{CH}$ bonded to two $\text{CH}_3$ groups and to $\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ (1-bromo-2-methylpropane).
